question: A title insurance policy protects the insured primarily against:
choice_a: Future declines in the property's market value
choice_b: Physical defects in the structure discovered after closing
choice_c: Financial loss arising from defects in title, liens, or encumbrances that existed but were undiscovered before the policy was issued
choice_d: The buyer's own future failure to pay property taxes
explanation: Title insurance is unusual among insurance products because it insures against past events — undisclosed defects, liens, or encumbrances that already existed before the policy's effective date — rather than future contingencies like a physical defect or a market decline.
source_note: General title insurance principle (Wikipedia 'Title insurance'); standard real-property-law concept taught in prelicensing courses nationwide.

question: Compared to most other forms of insurance, a title insurance policy is unusual in that it:
choice_a: Must be renewed annually with a rising premium
choice_b: Only covers losses that occur after the policy is issued
choice_c: Requires the insured to file a renewal claim every five years to maintain coverage
choice_d: Is purchased for a single, one-time premium paid at closing and, once issued, generally protects the insured for as long as they (or their heirs) retain the insured interest
explanation: Unlike auto or homeowner's insurance, title insurance is paid for with a single premium at closing rather than recurring premiums, reflecting that it insures against past title defects rather than ongoing future risk.
source_note: General title insurance premium structure (Wikipedia 'Title insurance'); standard settlement/closing practice.

question: Before issuing a title insurance policy, a title company performs a title search, which is best described as:
choice_a: An examination of the public land records to trace ownership history and identify any liens, encumbrances, or other matters affecting title
choice_b: A physical inspection of the property for structural defects
choice_c: An appraisal of the property's current market value
choice_d: A survey establishing the property's exact boundary lines
explanation: A title search is a records examination, not a physical inspection: the examiner reviews recorded deeds, mortgages, liens, judgments, and other instruments affecting the property to confirm the seller's ownership and reveal any defects before closing.
source_note: Title search process (Wikipedia 'Title insurance'; law.cornell.edu wex 'chain of title').

question: An abstract of title is best described as:
choice_a: The title insurance policy itself
choice_b: A condensed, chronological written summary of the recorded documents and events making up a property's chain of title
choice_c: A survey diagram of the parcel's boundaries
choice_d: A court order clearing all claims against a property
explanation: A title abstract is a summarized history of recorded conveyances, liens, and encumbrances affecting a parcel, compiled from the public records; it is distinct from — and often a precursor to — the title insurance policy itself.
source_note: Title abstract concept (law.cornell.edu wex 'chain of title'); standard title-examination terminology.

question: The 'chain of title' for a parcel of real property refers to:
choice_a: The sequence of liens currently attached to the property
choice_b: The list of easements benefiting the property
choice_c: The chronological history of recorded ownership transfers (deeds and other conveyances) from the earliest available owner up to the current owner
choice_d: The order in which mortgages on the property must be paid off
explanation: Chain of title is the historical record of successive ownership transfers of a parcel; a title company traces this chain to confirm the current seller actually holds valid, transferable ownership.
source_note: Chain of title definition (law.cornell.edu wex 'chain of title').

question: A 'cloud on title' refers to:
choice_a: A weather-related restriction on when a deed may be recorded
choice_b: A title insurance policy that has expired
choice_c: A minor survey discrepancy too small to affect value
choice_d: A recorded document, unreleased lien, or other claim that appears to impair an owner's title, even if it later proves invalid or unenforceable
explanation: A cloud on title is any outstanding claim, lien, or document of record that casts doubt on the owner's title, whether or not the claim ultimately turns out to be valid; it must generally be removed or resolved before title can be considered marketable.
source_note: Cloud on title concept, related to marketable title doctrine and quiet title actions (law.cornell.edu wex 'quiet title action').

question: A property owner discovers a decades-old, never-released mortgage lien still showing against her title, though the underlying debt was paid off long ago and the original lender no longer exists. Which legal action is designed to resolve this and establish clear ownership?
choice_a: A suit (action) to quiet title
choice_b: A partition action
choice_c: An unlawful detainer action
choice_d: A specific performance action
explanation: A quiet title action is a lawsuit brought against anyone who might claim an interest in the property, asking the court to resolve competing or clouded claims and issue a judgment establishing clear, marketable ownership.
source_note: Quiet title action purpose (law.cornell.edu wex 'quiet title action', citing Siskos v. Britz).

question: 'Marketable title' means title that is:
choice_a: Free of any mortgage regardless of whether it has been satisfied
choice_b: Reasonably free from material defects, encumbrances, or reasonable doubt as to its validity, such that a reasonably prudent buyer would be willing to accept it
choice_c: Recorded within the last 30 days
choice_d: Insured for at least the full replacement value of any structures on the property
explanation: Marketable (merchantable) title is title free enough from defects, liens, and reasonable doubt that a reasonably prudent, informed buyer would accept it without objection; it does not require literal perfection.
source_note: Marketable title standard, general real-property-law doctrine referenced across title-examination and quiet-title materials.

question: Standard title insurance policies typically list certain matters as exceptions from coverage unless a current survey is provided or extended coverage is purchased. Which of the following is a classic example of such a standard exception?
choice_a: A forged deed appearing in the chain of title
choice_b: The insured owner's own failure to pay the policy premium
choice_c: Matters a current, accurate survey would disclose, such as a boundary line encroachment
choice_d: A lien recorded after the policy's effective date
explanation: Standard title policies commonly exclude matters an accurate survey would reveal (like encroachments) and unrecorded rights of parties in possession, since these are outside what a records-based title search can uncover; extended coverage or a survey can remove such exceptions.
source_note: Standard title insurance policy exceptions, general ALTA-style policy convention (Wikipedia 'Title insurance').

question: A general warranty deed differs from a special (limited) warranty deed in that the general warranty deed's covenants of title:
choice_a: Apply only to defects arising during the current grantor's own period of ownership
choice_b: Provide no warranty of title whatsoever
choice_c: Apply only if the buyer separately purchases an owner's title insurance policy
choice_d: Extend back through the entire history of the property, warranting against title defects that arose at any time, even before the current grantor acquired it
explanation: A general warranty deed offers the broadest protection: the grantor warrants against title defects arising at any point in the property's history, not just during their own ownership, distinguishing it from a special warranty deed's narrower promise.
source_note: General vs. special warranty deed distinction (Wikipedia 'Deed'; standard real-property-law terminology).

question: In a general warranty deed, the covenant under which the grantor warrants that they actually own the estate being conveyed and have the legal right to convey it is the covenant of:
choice_a: Seisin
choice_b: Quiet enjoyment
choice_c: Further assurance
choice_d: Habendum
explanation: The covenant of seisin is the grantor's promise that they hold the very estate they purport to convey and possess the legal right to transfer it; a habendum clause, by contrast, is simply the 'to have and to hold' clause defining the estate granted.
source_note: Deed covenants of title, standard real-property-law terminology (general warranty deed covenants).

question: The covenant in a general warranty deed under which the grantor promises that the property is free of undisclosed liens, easements, or other encumbrances (other than those stated in the deed) is the covenant:
choice_a: Of seisin
choice_b: Against encumbrances
choice_c: Of further assurance
choice_d: Of the right to convey
explanation: The covenant against encumbrances is the grantor's assurance that no undisclosed liens, easements, restrictions, or other encumbrances burden the property except those specifically excepted in the deed.
source_note: Deed covenants of title, standard real-property-law terminology.

question: Under the covenant of quiet enjoyment in a general warranty deed, the grantor promises that:
choice_a: The grantee will never have to pay property taxes
choice_b: The grantor will personally guarantee the grantee's mortgage
choice_c: The grantee's possession of the property will not be disturbed by someone else asserting a superior, lawful claim to title
choice_d: The property will remain in good physical repair
explanation: The covenant of quiet enjoyment guarantees that the grantee's possession will not be disturbed by a third party's paramount claim of title; it addresses legal title disputes, not physical condition or financing.
source_note: Deed covenants of title, standard real-property-law terminology.

question: The covenant of further assurance in a general warranty deed obligates the grantor to:
choice_a: Refund the full purchase price automatically if any covenant is later breached
choice_b: Maintain title insurance on the grantee's behalf indefinitely
choice_c: Re-record the deed every ten years
choice_d: Perform any additional lawful acts reasonably necessary to correct defects and perfect the grantee's title
explanation: The covenant of further assurance requires the grantor to execute any additional documents or take further reasonable steps needed to cure defects and fully perfect the title conveyed to the grantee.
source_note: Deed covenants of title, standard real-property-law terminology.

question: A special (limited) warranty deed warrants title only against defects that:
choice_a: Arose during the grantor's own period of ownership, making no promises about what happened before the grantor acquired the property
choice_b: Arose at any point in the property's history, even before the grantor's own ownership
choice_c: Will arise after the sale closes
choice_d: Are already covered by the buyer's own title insurance policy
explanation: A special warranty deed limits the grantor's warranty to the period the grantor personally owned the property; it is common in commercial transactions and is frequently used by fiduciaries, corporate sellers, and lenders disposing of foreclosed (REO) property who lack knowledge of the property's earlier history.
source_note: Special/limited warranty deed scope and typical uses (Wikipedia 'Deed').

question: A quitclaim deed is often used to clear a minor cloud on title (for example, from a family member with an unclear or potential claim) because it:
choice_a: Guarantees the property is free of all defects
choice_b: Conveys only whatever interest, if any, the grantor currently holds, with no warranties of title whatsoever
choice_c: Cannot legally be used unless accompanied by title insurance
choice_d: Automatically extinguishes all prior liens on the property
explanation: A quitclaim deed transfers only the grantor's existing interest, if any, without any covenants or warranties about the quality of title; it is commonly used for family transfers, divorce settlements, and clearing potential claims rather than for arm's-length sales.
source_note: Quitclaim deed characteristics and typical uses (law.cornell.edu wex 'quitclaim deed').

question: A bargain and sale deed implies that the grantor:
choice_a: Warrants title against all defects, both past and present
choice_b: Has no interest whatsoever in the property being conveyed
choice_c: Holds and can convey title but makes no express warranties against encumbrances
choice_d: Must be a court-appointed official to use this deed form
explanation: A bargain and sale deed implies the grantor has and can convey the title but includes no express covenants against encumbrances; it is often used by fiduciaries, executors, and in tax sales or court-ordered conveyances.
source_note: Bargain and sale deed characteristics (Wikipedia 'Deed').

question: Which of the following is generally required for a deed to be legally valid?
choice_a: The grantee's signature
choice_b: Notarization by two separate notaries public
choice_c: A sale price equal to the property's appraised value
choice_d: A competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, words of conveyance (a granting clause), an adequate legal description, consideration, and the grantor's signature
explanation: A valid deed requires a legally competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, granting/conveyance language showing intent to transfer, an adequate legal description of the property, consideration, and the grantor's signature. The grantee generally does not need to sign a deed to accept it.
source_note: Essential elements of a valid deed (law.cornell.edu wex 'deed').

question: For a deed to be valid, the consideration recited in it:
choice_a: Can be nominal (such as '$10 and other good and valuable consideration') and need not reflect the property's actual value
choice_b: Must equal the property's full fair market value
choice_c: Must always be paid entirely in cash at the time of signing
choice_d: Is not required at all for the deed to be valid
explanation: Consideration is a required element of a valid deed, but it can be nominal — the recited amount does not need to reflect the true purchase price or market value of the property, especially in gift or family transfers.
source_note: Consideration requirement for a valid deed (law.cornell.edu wex 'deed').

question: Legal title to real property generally passes from grantor to grantee upon:
choice_a: The date the sales contract is signed
choice_b: Valid execution, delivery, and acceptance of the deed
choice_c: Recording of the deed in the public records
choice_d: Payment of the final loan installment
explanation: Title passes when a valid deed is executed, delivered by the grantor, and accepted by the grantee — recording is not required for title to pass between the parties, though it is essential to protect that title against later claimants.
source_note: When title passes: delivery and acceptance vs. recording (law.cornell.edu wex 'deed').

question: The primary legal effect of recording a deed in the public land records is to:
choice_a: Transfer title from grantor to grantee
choice_b: Automatically insure the grantee against all title defects
choice_c: Give constructive notice of the transfer to the world and establish the grantee's priority against later purchasers or creditors who might otherwise claim an interest in the property
choice_d: Convert the deed into a mortgage
explanation: Recording does not itself transfer title (that happens upon delivery and acceptance), but it puts the world on constructive notice of the conveyance and protects the grantee's priority against subsequent purchasers, lienholders, or creditors.
source_note: Purpose of recording and constructive notice doctrine (Wikipedia 'Recording (real estate)').

question: Under a 'race-notice' recording statute, used by most U.S. states, a later purchaser who pays value for the property will prevail over an earlier, unrecorded conveyance only if the later purchaser:
choice_a: Simply records first, regardless of whether they had notice of the earlier conveyance
choice_b: Had actual notice of the earlier conveyance
choice_c: Waits at least 30 days after purchase before recording
choice_d: Had no actual or constructive notice of the earlier conveyance and records first
explanation: A race-notice statute requires a subsequent bona fide purchaser to both lack notice of the prior conveyance and win the 'race' to record before the earlier purchaser does; most states use this hybrid approach, as opposed to pure race or pure notice statutes.
source_note: Race, notice, and race-notice recording statutes (Wikipedia 'Recording (real estate)').

question: If a valid deed is executed and delivered but never recorded, the conveyance is:
choice_a: Still valid and enforceable between the original grantor and grantee, though the grantee risks losing priority to a later bona fide purchaser who records first
choice_b: Void, and title never actually passed to the grantee
choice_c: Automatically converted into a lease
choice_d: Only enforceable if witnessed personally by a judge
explanation: An unrecorded deed is fully valid between the grantor and grantee; the risk of not recording is that a later bona fide purchaser for value, without notice, could record first and obtain superior rights under the applicable recording statute.
source_note: Effect of failing to record a valid deed (Wikipedia 'Recording (real estate)'; law.cornell.edu wex 'deed').

question: In a closing conducted through escrow, the escrow agent owes a fiduciary duty to:
choice_a: Only the buyer
choice_b: Both parties equally, following their mutual written escrow instructions rather than favoring either side
choice_c: Only the seller
choice_d: The listing broker's brokerage firm
explanation: An escrow agent acts as a neutral fiduciary for both the buyer and seller, holding funds and documents and disbursing/recording them strictly according to the parties' mutual written instructions, rather than advocating for either side.
source_note: Escrow agent's dual fiduciary role, standard escrow/closing practice.

question: The closing (settlement) statement prepared for a real estate transaction primarily serves to:
choice_a: Set the property's future resale price
choice_b: Replace the need for a deed
choice_c: Itemize the financial details of the transaction, including purchase price, loan proceeds, prorations, and all credits and debits charged to the buyer and seller
choice_d: Establish the property's assessed value for tax purposes
explanation: The closing statement (whether a Closing Disclosure, HUD-1, or similar settlement form) itemizes every financial component of the transaction so both parties can see exactly what each owes and receives at closing.
source_note: Closing/settlement statement function, standard real estate closing practice.

question: Since the TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure (TRID) rule took effect, the HUD-1 Settlement Statement has largely been replaced by the Closing Disclosure for most closed-end mortgage purchases. The HUD-1 (or HUD-1A) form, however, is still used for transactions such as:
choice_a: Standard 30-year fixed-rate purchase-money mortgages
choice_b: All-cash purchases involving no financing at all
choice_c: VA-guaranteed purchase loans exclusively
choice_d: Reverse mortgages and certain open-end home equity lines of credit
explanation: TRID's Closing Disclosure replaced the HUD-1 for most closed-end consumer mortgage purchases and refinances, but the HUD-1/HUD-1A remains in use for transaction types TRID does not cover, such as reverse mortgages and open-end home equity lines of credit.
source_note: HUD-1 Settlement Statement current scope of use (Wikipedia 'HUD-1 Settlement Statement').

question: A seller has already paid the full year's property taxes of $3,650 in advance for the calendar year. If closing occurs exactly 100 days before the end of that tax year, prorating the taxes at closing (using a 365-day year) would generally result in:
choice_a: A credit to the seller and a corresponding debit to the buyer, for the buyer's share of the prepaid taxes covering the 100 days remaining in the year
choice_b: The seller owing the buyer nothing, since taxes are non-refundable
choice_c: A credit to the buyer only, with no offsetting debit to anyone
choice_d: The taxing authority refunding the buyer directly at year-end
explanation: The daily tax rate is $3,650 / 365 = $10/day. Since the seller prepaid the full year but will only own the property for the days before closing, the buyer owes the seller for the 100 days of the prepaid period the buyer will actually own the property (100 x $10 = $1,000): a credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer.
source_note: Standard property tax proration calculation used in closing/settlement statements.

question: A tax imposed by a state or local government on the privilege of transferring real property, typically calculated as a percentage of the sale price and evidenced by stamps or a fee affixed to the deed, is known as a:
choice_a: Ad valorem property tax
choice_b: Real estate transfer (documentary stamp) tax
choice_c: Capital gains tax
choice_d: Mortgage recording tax on the buyer's new loan
explanation: A real estate transfer tax (also called a documentary stamp tax or conveyance tax) is charged on the transfer of real property itself, generally based on the sale price; whether the buyer, seller, or both pay it varies by state and local custom, and some states impose none at all.
source_note: Real estate transfer tax mechanics and variation by jurisdiction (Wikipedia 'Real estate transfer tax').

question: Which of the following is most accurately classified as a 'closing cost' rather than part of the negotiated purchase price itself?
choice_a: The earnest money deposit
choice_b: The seller's original asking price
choice_c: Title insurance premiums, recording fees, and loan origination charges paid to complete the transaction
choice_d: The appraised value of the home
explanation: Closing costs are the various fees and charges — such as title insurance premiums, recording fees, transfer taxes, and loan origination charges — incurred to complete the transaction, separate from the negotiated purchase price of the property itself.
source_note: Standard closing cost categories, real estate closing practice.

question: For federal income tax purposes, a homeowner who itemizes deductions may generally deduct which of the following, subject to applicable IRS limits?
choice_a: The full purchase price of the home in the year it was purchased
choice_b: Homeowners association dues
choice_c: Estimated future appreciation in the home's value
choice_d: Mortgage interest paid on qualifying acquisition debt and state and local property taxes
explanation: Itemizing homeowners may generally deduct mortgage interest on qualifying acquisition debt and state and local property taxes (subject to the SALT cap and other IRS limits); the purchase price itself, HOA dues, and unrealized appreciation are not deductible.
source_note: General federal income tax treatment of homeownership costs (IRS guidance on itemized deductions).

question: Under IRC Section 121, an individual who sells their primary residence may generally exclude how much of the capital gain from federal income tax, provided the ownership-and-use tests are met?
choice_a: $250,000 for a single filer ($500,000 for a married couple filing jointly)
choice_d: There is no exclusion available on the sale of a primary residence
explanation: IRC Section 121 lets a qualifying single filer exclude up to $250,000 of capital gain (and a married couple filing jointly up to $500,000) on the sale of a principal residence, provided the ownership and use tests are satisfied.
source_note: IRC Section 121 home sale exclusion amounts (IRS Topic No. 701, irs.gov).

question: To qualify for the Section 121 home-sale capital gains exclusion, a seller must generally have owned and used the property as a principal residence for:
choice_a: At least 6 months immediately before the sale
choice_b: At least 2 of the 5 years immediately preceding the sale
choice_c: At least 10 consecutive years
choice_d: The entire time the seller has owned any real property
explanation: The Section 121 exclusion requires the seller to meet both an ownership test and a use test: owning and using the home as a principal residence for at least 2 of the 5 years ending on the date of sale (the two periods need not be identical).
source_note: IRC Section 121 ownership and use tests (IRS Topic No. 701, irs.gov).

question: In calculating the taxable capital gain on the sale of real property, a seller's 'adjusted basis' generally equals:
choice_a: The property's current market value only
choice_b: The outstanding mortgage balance at the time of sale
choice_c: The original purchase price, plus the cost of qualifying capital improvements, minus any allowable depreciation taken
choice_d: The county's assessed value used for property tax purposes
explanation: Adjusted basis starts with the original cost of acquiring the property, is increased by qualifying capital improvements, and is reduced by any depreciation claimed (for investment or business use); capital gain is the sale price less selling costs and this adjusted basis.
source_note: Adjusted basis calculation for capital gains, general federal income tax treatment of real property sales.

question: An investor selling business or investment real property may defer paying capital gains tax on the transaction by structuring it as a:
choice_a: Section 121 principal residence exclusion
choice_b: Short sale
choice_c: Deed in lieu of foreclosure
choice_d: Section 1031 like-kind exchange for other qualifying investment or business real property
explanation: A Section 1031 like-kind exchange allows an investor to defer capital gains tax by exchanging business or investment real property for other qualifying like-kind real property, rather than recognizing the gain immediately in a taxable sale.
source_note: IRC Section 1031 like-kind exchange concept, general federal tax treatment of investment real property.

question: A property becomes classified as 'REO' (real estate owned) when:
choice_a: No third party submits a winning bid covering the outstanding debt at the foreclosure sale, so the foreclosing lender takes title to the property itself
choice_b: A buyer purchases it directly from an individual seller
choice_c: The seller lists the property exclusively with one brokerage
choice_d: The property passes through a Section 1031 exchange
explanation: When a foreclosure auction fails to attract a bid at least equal to the debt owed — often because the debt exceeds market value — the foreclosing lender takes title itself, and the property becomes 'real estate owned' (REO), a non-earning asset on the lender's books.
source_note: REO definition and how it arises (Wikipedia 'Real estate owned').

question: Compared to a typical resale listing, an REO (bank-owned) property is most often marketed and sold:
choice_a: With a full seller's disclosure of latent defects and extensive seller-funded repair credits
choice_b: 'As-is,' with the lender (often through an asset manager or listing broker) seeking to recover as much of its loss as the market will bear, and with lender-specific contract addenda
choice_c: Only through sealed-bid public auctions conducted directly by a court
choice_d: With an automatic general warranty deed guaranteeing clear title back to the date of original construction
explanation: Lenders holding REO property typically sell through a broker or in-house asset management department, market the property 'as-is' with minimal disclosures, and use lender-drafted addenda, aiming to recover as much of the unpaid loan balance as the market supports.
source_note: REO disposition practices (Wikipedia 'Real estate owned').

question: In a short sale, before the transaction can close, the borrower's lender(s) must generally:
choice_a: Automatically approve any offer above the original loan amount
choice_b: Foreclose on the property before any offer can be considered
choice_c: Approve the sale, since the net proceeds will be insufficient to fully satisfy the outstanding lien(s), and the lienholder must agree to release its lien for less than the amount owed
choice_d: Transfer the loan to a different servicer before any offer can be considered
explanation: A short sale requires lender approval because the sale price will not generate enough proceeds to pay off the mortgage debt in full; the lienholder must consent to release its lien and accept less than the full amount owed for the sale to close.
source_note: Short sale approval mechanics, standard real estate finance terminology for pre-foreclosure alternatives.

question: When a lender forgives all or part of a borrower's mortgage debt in connection with a short sale or foreclosure, that forgiven amount:
choice_a: Is never taxable under any circumstances
choice_b: Automatically becomes a tax credit for the lender only
choice_c: Must be repaid to the lender in full within one year regardless of the sale
choice_d: May be treated as taxable 'cancellation of debt' (COD) income and reported to the borrower and the IRS on Form 1099-C, unless an exclusion applies
explanation: Forgiven mortgage debt is generally treated as income to the borrower under the tax law concept of 'accession to wealth,' and a creditor canceling $600 or more must report it on Form 1099-C, though exclusions (such as insolvency or bankruptcy) can eliminate the tax liability.
source_note: Cancellation of debt (COD) income and Form 1099-C reporting (general federal income tax treatment of forgiven mortgage debt).

question: A borrower whose total debts exceeded the fair market value of their assets immediately before mortgage debt was cancelled in a short sale may be able to exclude the resulting cancellation-of-debt income from taxable income under the:
choice_a: Insolvency exclusion (or, where applicable, the bankruptcy or qualified principal residence indebtedness exclusions)
choice_b: Section 121 principal residence exclusion
choice_c: Section 1031 like-kind exchange
choice_d: Homestead exemption
explanation: A taxpayer who was insolvent immediately before the debt cancellation (liabilities exceeding assets) can exclude cancellation-of-debt income up to the amount of that insolvency; debt discharged in bankruptcy is also excluded, and other targeted exclusions may apply to qualifying principal residence debt.
source_note: Insolvency and related exclusions from cancellation-of-debt income (general federal income tax treatment).

question: The deed issued to the successful bidder at a non-judicial (power-of-sale) foreclosure auction, conveying whatever title the borrower had without any warranties of title, is generally called a:
choice_a: General warranty deed
choice_b: Trustee's deed (deed upon sale)
choice_c: Gift deed
choice_d: Reconveyance deed
explanation: After a non-judicial foreclosure sale, the trustee conveys the property to the successful bidder by a trustee's deed (deed upon sale), which passes whatever title the borrower held but, like a quitclaim deed, carries no warranties of title.
source_note: Trustee's deed upon sale, standard non-judicial foreclosure terminology distinct from a reconveyance deed (issued when a debt is paid off, not sold).
